title: American Mining Congress v. Mine Safety and Health Administration (1993)
shortTitle: American Mining Congress v. Mine Safety and Health Administration (1993)
summary: The court identified circumstances showing that an agency exercised legislative power rather than merely interpreted existing law.
notes: The underlying dispute concerned three MSHA Program Policy Letters, issued without notice and comment and not published in the Federal Register, stating when chest x-ray readings count as a 'diagnosis' of lung disease that mine operators must report under the Part 50 regulations; the court's test asks (1) whether without the rule there would be no adequate legislative basis for enforcement, (2) whether the agency published the rule in the C.F.R., (3) whether the agency explicitly invoked its general legislative authority, and (4) whether the rule effectively amends a prior legislative rule, with a 'yes' to any making the rule legislative; the court held the PPLs interpretive.

sections.Parties: The caption identifies American Mining Congress and the Mine Safety and Health Administration. The assigned discussion uses the decision to explain classification of interpretive rules without supplying the particular mining dispute.
sections.Material Facts: The court considered how to identify a rule with the force of law. Its examples addressed a statute that supplies no enforceable duty until an agency makes a rule, agency publication practices, and a later pronouncement inconsistent with an existing legislative rule. These are illustrations in the excerpt rather than a reconstructed account of the underlying controversy.
sections.Procedural History: The D.C. Circuit decided the case in 1993.
sections.Issue: What indicates that a purported interpretation is instead an exercise of delegated legislative authority?
sections.Holding: The excerpt identifies several indicators of legislative action, especially whether an adequate legal basis for enforcement exists without the new rule and whether the rule amends or contradicts an existing legislative rule. The underlying mandate is omitted.
sections.Reasoning: An interpretation draws its legal basis from an existing statute or rule. If no duty exists until the agency supplies it, the agency is using delegated lawmaking power. Likewise, repudiating a legislative rule generally requires a legislative amendment. The decision also listed publication in the Code of Federal Regulations, but the casebook expressly reports that the circuit later removed that indicator. The notes caution that these indicators identify clear cases without deciding every instance in which they are absent. They also distinguish force of law in this inquiry from the practical-binding-effect inquiry used for policy statements; an interpretation’s real consequences do not alone establish new legislation.

topics.lrs-n-interpretive-rules: The need to supply a previously missing legal duty, or to amend a legislative rule, indicates legislative action.
topics.lrs-n-guidance: The Program Policy Letters were guidance documents, and the case supplies the leading test for when guidance is really a legislative rule requiring notice and comment.
topics.lrs-o-section-553: The four-part test decides whether the § 553(b)(A) exemption for interpretive rules applies.
